title: MoBA-Adapt: Dynamic Block Granularity Adaptation in Mixture of Block Attention for Heterogeneous Long-Context Tasks
description:
Problem: MoBA uses fixed-size blocks for sparse attention routing, but optimal block granularity varies significantly across task types (e.g., fine-grained retrieval needs small blocks, high-level reasoning benefits from coarser blocks) and even across layers within the same model. A static block size introduces a fundamental mismatch that limits performance on diverse long-context workloads.

Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Adapt, which extends MoBA with a lightweight meta-routing module that dynamically selects block granularity per layer and per input sequence. Specifically, we define a hierarchical block vocabulary (e.g., 128, 512, 2048 tokens), and train a small MLP-based granularity selector that takes layer index and a compressed sequence representation as input, outputting a soft mixture over granularities. The attention computation proceeds using the selected granularity, with gradient-straight-through estimators enabling end-to-end training. A regularization term encourages diversity across layers to prevent granularity collapse.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark on RULER, LongBench, and Needle-in-Haystack across 32K–512K context lengths; (2) Ablation over fixed vs. adaptive granularity at matched FLOPs; (3) Analysis of learned granularity distributions per layer and task type; (4) Inference throughput comparison against MoBA and full attention baselines. We expect 5-12% accuracy gains on heterogeneous task suites with comparable or improved latency.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Block Granularity Selection in Mixture of Block Attention for Heterogeneous Long-Context Tasks
description: Problem: MoBA uses fixed-size blocks when partitioning the context for sparse attention routing. However, optimal block granularity varies significantly across tasks—code understanding benefits from fine-grained token-level attention within functions, while document summarization operates better with coarse paragraph-level blocks. Fixed block sizes force a suboptimal trade-off across diverse workloads. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiMoBA, which extends MoBA with a hierarchical multi-granularity block structure. Each attention head independently selects both which blocks to attend to AND at what granularity (e.g., 128, 512, or 2048 token blocks), using a lightweight two-stage router: a granularity selector followed by a block selector at the chosen resolution. The granularity selector is trained with a differentiable soft-selection mechanism with an entropy regularization term encouraging diversity across heads. This allows the model to learn task-adaptive attention patterns without manual configuration. Planned Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, InfiniteBench, LongBench comparing against MoBA, NSA, and full attention baselines; (2) Ablations on granularity diversity regularization strength; (3) Analysis of learned granularity distributions per task type and layer depth; (4) Efficiency profiling (FLOPs, wall-clock time) at 32K–256K context lengths on 7B and 70B model scales.

title: AdaptMoBA: Dynamic Expert Count Allocation in Mixture of Block Attention via Complexity-Aware Routing
description: Problem: MoBA uses a fixed number of attended blocks (top-k) regardless of query complexity, creating a uniform computational budget across tokens. Simple tokens waste capacity by attending k blocks while complex reasoning tokens may be starved of context. Method: We propose AdaptMoBA, which learns to dynamically allocate the number of attended blocks per query token based on an estimated 'contextual complexity score.' A lightweight auxiliary network predicts per-token complexity from query representations, outputting a variable k_i ∈ [k_min, k_max] for each token. We impose a global budget constraint via a differentiable soft threshold, ensuring average attended blocks equals a target k_avg while allowing flexibility per token. We also introduce a complexity-aware load balancing loss to prevent routing collapse. The transition to full attention is preserved by setting k_max = total blocks. Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks (SCROLLS, LongBench, RULER) comparing fixed-k MoBA vs AdaptMoBA at matched average FLOPs; (2) Multi-hop reasoning tasks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHop) where complexity variation is high; (3) Ablations on k_min/k_max ranges and budget constraints; (4) Analysis of learned complexity distributions across token types; (5) Throughput measurements on 128K context lengths. We expect 3-8% accuracy gains on reasoning tasks with identical average compute.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Expert Count Allocation in Mixture of Block Attention via Complexity-Aware Routing
description:
Problem: MoBA assigns a fixed number of block experts per query token regardless of the local complexity of the input. Simple passages (repetitive text, padding-heavy sequences) waste compute attending to K blocks, while semantically dense or multi-hop reasoning segments may be under-attended with the same budget. This mismatch between fixed routing capacity and variable input complexity limits efficiency gains in heterogeneous long-document workloads (e.g., legal contracts interleaved with tables, code repositories with docstrings).

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiMoBA, which augments MoBA's router with a lightweight complexity predictor (a small MLP operating on query token representations) that outputs a per-token expert count k_i drawn from a discrete set {1,2,...,K_max}. A differentiable straight-through estimator enables end-to-end training. A load-balancing auxiliary loss encourages diversity of k_i selections across the sequence. During inference, tokens are binned by k_i and processed in parallel batches, preserving hardware efficiency.

Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: RULER, InfiniteBench, LongBench; (2) Ablations on fixed-k vs. adaptive-k at matched average FLOPs; (3) Analysis of k_i distributions across document types (code, narrative, tabular); (4) Throughput/latency profiling on A100s for 32K–256K contexts; (5) Needle-in-haystack and multi-hop QA to verify reasoning fidelity is preserved.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Expert Count Adaptation in Mixture of Block Attention for Heterogeneous Long-Context Tasks
description: Problem: MoBA uses a fixed number of attended blocks (top-k selection) regardless of query complexity or context length, leading to suboptimal compute allocation — simple factual retrievals waste capacity attending k blocks while complex multi-hop reasoning tasks may need more. We also introduce a block granularity scheduler that coarsens/refines block sizes based on estimated query locality. title: AdaptiveMoBA: Dynamic Expert Count Scheduling for Mixture of Block Attention Based on Query Complexity
description:
Problem: MoBA uses a fixed number of attended blocks (top-k selection) regardless of query complexity. Simple queries (factual retrieval) may need only 1-2 blocks while complex multi-hop reasoning may require attending to many dispersed blocks. A static k wastes computation on simple queries and under-allocates for complex ones, suboptimally trading accuracy for efficiency.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveMoBA, which augments MoBA's router with a lightweight 'complexity estimator' — a small MLP head that predicts per-query optimal k from the query hidden state and current context statistics (e.g., entropy of router scores distribution). During training, we use a differentiable soft-k selection via a learned threshold on router logits, with a regularization loss encouraging sparse k for low-entropy routing distributions. At inference, k is dynamically set per query within a pre-defined budget envelope [k_min, k_max].

Experiments: (1) Benchmark on SCROLLS, LongBench, and RULER across 32K-512K context lengths comparing fixed-k MoBA vs. AdaptiveMoBA at equivalent average FLOPs; (2) Ablation on complexity estimator design (entropy-based vs. learned); (3) Analysis of k-distribution correlations with query types (retrieval vs. reasoning vs. summarization); (4) Throughput/latency profiling on A100 GPUs. We expect 8-15% accuracy improvement on multi-hop reasoning tasks at matched compute budgets.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Block Granularity in Mixture of Block Attention for Heterogeneous Long-Context Tasks
description:

Legal documents benefit from fine-grained sentence-level blocks, while code repositories need coarse file-level blocks. A static block size forces a suboptimal compromise across heterogeneous inputs.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiMoBA, which augments MoBA with a lightweight hierarchical block segmentation mechanism that dynamically determines block boundaries and sizes per layer per input. Specifically, a small boundary predictor network (trained jointly end-to-end) segments the sequence into variable-length blocks based on local semantic coherence signals (e.g., embedding similarity deltas). The MoE routing then operates over these adaptive blocks. We further introduce a multi-granularity routing scheme where different attention heads can select blocks at different granularity levels (fine/medium/coarse), allowing simultaneous local and global reasoning.

Experiments: (1) Compare against fixed-block MoBA and other sparse attention baselines on RULER, LongBench, and InfiniteBench. (2) Ablate block granularity levels and routing strategies. (3) Analyze learned block boundaries on heterogeneous corpora (code, legal text, scientific papers). (4) Measure FLOPs-vs-accuracy tradeoffs at 32K, 128K, and 512K context lengths. (5) Fine-tune a 7B model from a MoBA checkpoint to evaluate transfer efficiency.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Expert Count Allocation in Mixture of Block Attention for Heterogeneous Long-Context Tasks
description:
Problem: MoBA uses a fixed number of attended blocks (top-k selection) across all attention heads and all tokens uniformly, ignoring that different query tokens and layers likely require vastly different amounts of context—a named entity resolution may need 2 blocks while complex multi-hop reasoning may need 10. This static allocation wastes capacity for simple tokens and under-serves complex ones.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiMoBA, which learns per-token, per-layer dynamic k-selection via a lightweight auxiliary predictor network. Given a query vector, a small MLP predicts a token-specific budget k_i from a discrete set {1,2,4,8,...,K_max}, trained with a differentiable budget regularization loss that balances task performance against FLOPs. We additionally propose a 'block merging' strategy where adjacent high-scoring blocks are merged into larger attended regions, preserving locality while reducing routing overhead.

Experiments: (1) Benchmarks on SCROLLS, LongBench, and RULER across 32K–512K context lengths comparing MoBA (fixed-k), full attention, and AdaptiMoBA. (2) Analysis of learned k distributions per layer and token type (reasoning vs. factual retrieval tasks). (3) Ablation of the auxiliary predictor capacity and regularization strength. (4) Throughput/accuracy Pareto curves against NSA and MoBA baselines. We target 15-25% FLOPs reduction over MoBA at matched accuracy.

title: AdaptiBA: Adaptive Block Allocation for MoBA via Learned Query-Aware Block Sizing
description: Problem: MoBA assumes uniform block partitioning of the context window, but information density in long documents is highly non-uniform—dense reasoning chains, code, or tables may require finer-grained attention while narrative passages can tolerate coarser blocks. Fixed block sizes force a trade-off between granularity and efficiency that cannot adapt to content structure. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiBA, which replaces MoBA's static uniform blocks with dynamically sized blocks determined by a lightweight boundary predictor trained end-to-end. The predictor operates on key representations to identify natural semantic boundaries (paragraph breaks, logical steps, entity transitions), producing variable-length blocks. The MoE-style routing then selects among these semantically coherent blocks rather than fixed positional chunks. A differentiable relaxation during training allows gradient flow through boundary decisions. At inference, block boundaries are computed once per forward pass with negligible overhead. Planned Experiments: (1) Perplexity on long-document benchmarks (SCROLLS, LongBench) comparing AdaptiBA vs. MoBA vs. full attention across 32K-256K context lengths; (2) Needle-in-a-haystack retrieval accuracy measuring whether semantic blocks improve routing precision; (3) FLOP analysis showing efficiency gains from fewer, larger blocks in low-density regions; (4) Ablation on boundary predictor architectures and routing temperature; (5) Fine-tuning from a MoBA-pretrained checkpoint to validate compatibility.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Block Granularity in Mixture of Block Attention for Heterogeneous Long-Document Tasks

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Block Granularity in Mixture of Block Attention via Reinforcement Learning
description:

Coarse blocks waste capacity on fine-grained reasoning tasks, while fine blocks increase routing overhead on retrieval-heavy tasks. No principled method exists to adapt block sizes dynamically during inference or training.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiMoBA, which learns per-layer, per-head block granularity policies using a lightweight meta-controller trained via reinforcement learning. The meta-controller observes attention entropy statistics and positional distance distributions from recent forward passes, then selects from a discrete set of block sizes (e.g., 128, 512, 2048 tokens). A differentiable relaxation enables joint training with the base LLM. We additionally propose a hierarchical block decomposition: coarse blocks for initial routing, with fine-grained sub-block attention applied only within selected blocks for high-complexity reasoning regions.

Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, LongBench, RULER across 32K–1M token contexts. (2) Ablations on fixed vs. adaptive granularity per task type. (3) FLOPs/latency vs. accuracy Pareto curves comparing against MoBA, StreamingLLM, and LongFormer. (4) Analysis of emergent granularity patterns across layers and task domains to understand what the policy learns.

title: AdaptiBA: Adaptive Block Allocation for MoBA via Learned Query Complexity Estimation

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Expert Count Scheduling in Mixture of Block Attention for Variable-Length Long-Context Inference
description:

We add a sparsity regularization loss to encourage low-k selections for simple tokens while allowing high-k for complex ones. A global FLOPs budget is enforced per layer via a soft constraint averaged across tokens in a batch.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Expert Granularity in Mixture of Block Attention via Learned Block Sizing

The predictor, a small 2-layer MLP operating on token representations, outputs soft boundary probabilities trained end-to-end via a differentiable segmentation via Gumbel-Softmax. A regularization term encourages a target mean block size while permitting high variance. Each dynamically formed block then participates in standard MoBA routing. Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, LongBench, RULER at 32K–256K tokens; (2) Ablation comparing fixed vs. adaptive block sizes across document types (code, legal, scientific); (3) Efficiency analysis measuring FLOPs and wall-clock time versus MoBA and full attention baselines; (4) Interpretability study visualizing learned block boundaries against human-annotated discourse segments to validate semantic alignment.

title: HierMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention for Multi-Document Reasoning
description: Problem: MoBA's block-based routing treats all token blocks uniformly, missing the natural hierarchical structure in multi-document long-context tasks (e.g., legal corpora, scientific literature review, multi-hop QA). Queries often need to first identify relevant documents, then attend to specific passages within them—a two-level retrieval process that flat block routing cannot efficiently exploit. Proposed Method: We introduce HierMoBA, a two-level sparse attention architecture where a coarse-grained router first selects relevant document-level super-blocks using learned document embeddings (e.g., CLS-token aggregations), then a fine-grained MoBA-style router selects token-level blocks within selected super-blocks. The hierarchical routing is differentiable via straight-through Gumbel-softmax estimation, allowing end-to-end training. We augment block boundaries to align with document delimiters when available, and fall back to fixed-size blocks otherwise. A lightweight document-summarization auxiliary loss encourages informative super-block representations. Experiments: (1) Multi-hop QA benchmarks (MuSiQue, HotpotQA-full-wiki) at 128K context; (2) Long-document summarization (SCROLLS, QASPER); (3) Legal multi-document reasoning (CUAD); (4) Ablations on routing levels, super-block sizes, and comparison against MoBA, MInference, and full attention baselines. We measure accuracy, FLOPs, and routing entropy to evaluate efficiency-performance tradeoffs.

title: HieraMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention with Adaptive Granularity for Multi-Scale Long-Context Reasoning
description:
Problem: MoBA assigns queries to fixed-size blocks uniformly, but real-world long-context tasks (e.g., multi-hop reasoning over documents, code repositories) exhibit multi-scale dependency structures — some queries need fine-grained token-level attention while others benefit from coarse paragraph-level summaries. A single block granularity creates a mismatch that either wastes compute on irrelevant tokens or misses cross-scale dependencies.

Proposed Method: We introduce HieraMoBA, which maintains a hierarchy of block sizes (e.g., 128, 512, 2048 tokens) and learns a two-level routing mechanism: (1) a granularity router selects which scale(s) each query head should operate at, and (2) a block router (MoE-style) selects top-K blocks within each chosen scale. Block representations at coarser levels are computed via lightweight learned pooling updated incrementally. The granularity router is trained with a differentiable load-balancing loss encouraging diversity across scales.

Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, LongBench, RULER at 32K–256K contexts; (2) Multi-hop QA (HotpotQA-long, MuSiQue) isolating cross-scale reasoning gains; (3) Ablations on number of hierarchy levels and block sizes; (4) Throughput/FLOPs comparison vs. MoBA, full attention, and StreamingLLM; (5) Analysis of granularity router behavior across task types to validate multi-scale hypothesis.

title: HierMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention with Adaptive Granularity for Multi-Scale Long-Context Reasoning
description: Problem: MoBA partitions context into fixed-size blocks, but real-world long documents exhibit multi-scale structure (sentences, paragraphs, sections). Each query first routes through a coarse-grained MoE gating to identify relevant sections, then refines attention within selected sections using finer granularity. Block representations at coarser levels are computed as learned pooling over finer blocks, updated incrementally during inference. A lightweight router predicts the appropriate granularity mix per query head, enabling adaptive attention spans without manual tuning. Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, RULER, LongBench comparing against MoBA, sliding window, and full attention baselines; (2) Ablations on granularity hierarchy depth and routing strategies; (3) Needle-in-a-haystack tests up to 512K tokens; (4) Efficiency profiling (FLOPs, latency) on 7B and 70B models; (5) Analysis of emergent routing patterns to verify semantic alignment of selected blocks.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Block Granularity in Mixture of Block Attention for Heterogeneous Long-Context Reasoning
description:

title: HieraMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention with Adaptive Granularity for Multi-Scale Long-Document Reasoning

title: MoBA-Grad: Differentiable Block Routing for End-to-End Sparse Attention Learning
description:

We augment the router with a lightweight learned MLP that combines query embeddings with positional block metadata (recency, frequency statistics), trained jointly with the attention parameters. During inference, we anneal to hard discrete routing for efficiency. We additionally introduce a load-balancing auxiliary loss adapted for attention blocks rather than expert tokens.

Experiments: (1) Compare perplexity and long-context benchmark performance (RULER, LongBench, BABILong) against vanilla MoBA and full attention baselines at 32K-128K context lengths; (2) Ablate routing mechanisms (similarity-only vs. learned MLP vs. combined); (3) Analyze learned routing patterns via attention block activation heatmaps to interpret emergent structure; (4) Evaluate multi-hop reasoning tasks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA) where non-local dependencies are critical; (5) Measure training convergence speed and FLOPs trade-offs.

title: HierMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention with Adaptive Granularity for Multi-Scale Long-Context Reasoning

title: MoBA-Graph: Adaptive Block Attention Routing for Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Knowledge Graphs
description: Problem: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over large knowledge graphs (KGs) requires attending to semantically distant but logically connected entities scattered across long contexts. Standard sparse attention methods like MoBA partition context into contiguous blocks, but KG-linearized inputs have non-contiguous relational structure, causing relevant entity mentions to be split across poorly-routed blocks. Proposed Method: We extend MoBA's MoE-inspired gating mechanism with a graph-topology-aware routing objective. Each query computes block affinities using both content similarity and a lightweight graph proximity signal derived from entity co-occurrence embeddings injected into block representations. The router learns to select blocks containing related entities even when they are positionally distant, while preserving MoBA's ability to fall back to full attention during fine-tuning. A new 'entity bridge' token is inserted at KG triple boundaries to anchor block boundaries to semantic units rather than fixed token counts. Experiments: (1) Multi-hop QA benchmarks (MuSiQue, HotpotQA) with KG-linearized contexts up to 128K tokens; (2) Ablation comparing fixed-block MoBA vs. graph-guided routing on retrieval accuracy and reasoning F1; (3) Efficiency profiling (FLOPs, latency) vs. full attention and vanilla MoBA; (4) Generalization to biomedical KG QA (PrimeKG). We expect 5-8% F1 improvement over MoBA on multi-hop tasks with comparable efficiency.

title: MoBA-Tree: Hierarchical Block Attention Routing for Ultra-Long Document Reasoning
description:
Problem: MoBA assigns queries to flat blocks of fixed size, treating all context positions uniformly. For ultra-long documents (1M+ tokens) with inherent hierarchical structure (sentences → paragraphs → sections → documents), flat block routing wastes routing capacity on irrelevant granularities and misses semantic coherence within natural document boundaries.

Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Tree, a hierarchical attention routing mechanism that builds a multi-level block tree over the context. At inference time, each query first routes to coarse-grained 'super-blocks' (e.g., sections) via a lightweight router, then recursively selects fine-grained blocks within chosen super-blocks. Routing is learned end-to-end using differentiable top-k selection with straight-through estimators at each tree level. The hierarchy is constructed dynamically using document structure signals (e.g., special tokens, semantic embeddings) or fixed geometric splits as fallback. This yields O(log N) routing decisions per query while maintaining sparse O(k log N) attention complexity.

Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, InfiniteBench, RULER at 128K–1M tokens; (2) Ablation on hierarchy depth and block size schedules; (3) Routing interpretability analysis showing alignment with document structure; (4) Wall-clock efficiency vs. MoBA, full attention, and StreamingLLM; (5) Fine-tuning from pre-trained MoBA checkpoints to measure adaptation cost.

title: AdaptiBA: Adaptive Block Allocation for Heterogeneous Long-Context Reasoning Tasks
description: Problem: MoBA treats all attention heads and layers uniformly when routing queries to blocks, yet empirical evidence suggests different layers and heads specialize in distinct linguistic phenomena (syntax, coreference, factual retrieval). This uniformity wastes capacity—shallow layers may benefit from local window attention while deep reasoning layers need flexible long-range access. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Block Attention (AdaptiBA), which augments MoBA with a lightweight per-layer, per-head meta-router that dynamically adjusts both the number of attended blocks (k) and the block granularity based on layer depth and a learned head-type classifier. Specifically: (1) we train a small MLP meta-controller that predicts optimal k per head given layer index and running attention entropy statistics; (2) we introduce hierarchical block sizes—fine-grained blocks in upper layers, coarse in lower—allowing variable-resolution long-range attention; (3) we add a differentiable block-budget regularizer penalizing per-layer FLOPs, enabling explicit compute-accuracy tradeoffs at inference. Experiments: We evaluate on SCROLLS, RULER, and LongBench benchmarks using Llama-3-8B and Mistral-7B backbones, comparing against MoBA, StreamingLLM, and BigBird. Ablations isolate contributions of adaptive-k, hierarchical blocks, and budget regularization. We also profile per-layer attention entropy to validate head specialization hypotheses.

title: MoBA-Graph: Adaptive Block Attention Routing for Graph-Structured Long Documents
description: Problem: Long documents often have latent graph structure (e.g., legal contracts referencing clauses, scientific papers citing sections, codebases with function dependencies). MoBA's block routing is purely positional, ignoring semantic connectivity that could dramatically improve sparse attention quality on structured long-context inputs. Proposed Method: We extend MoBA by incorporating document graph structure into the gating mechanism. A lightweight graph encoder (GNN) processes a pre-extracted entity/section dependency graph and produces node embeddings. These embeddings augment the standard query-based block routing scores in MoBA's MoE gating, biasing attention toward blocks that are both semantically similar and structurally connected. Crucially, the graph is extracted cheaply via off-the-shelf parsers (e.g., citation extractors, AST parsers) and the GNN adds minimal overhead. The model retains MoBA's ability to fall back to full attention. Experiments: (1) Long legal document QA (ContractNLI, CUAD) where clause cross-references are explicit; (2) Multi-file code understanding (SWE-bench style tasks); (3) Scientific paper multi-hop QA (QASPER, MuSiQue-long). Ablations compare: positional-only MoBA, graph-only routing, combined hybrid, and full attention baselines. We measure accuracy, routing entropy (sparsity quality), and FLOPs at 32K–128K context lengths. Expected outcome: graph-augmented routing achieves 8-15% accuracy gains over positional MoBA on structured documents with equivalent efficiency.

title: MoBA-Edit: Sparse Block Attention for Efficient Long-Document Editing and Revision via Targeted Context Retrieval
description:
Problem: Long-document editing (e.g., revising a 100K-token technical report or legal contract) requires an LLM to attend to both local edit context and semantically relevant distant passages—a fundamentally different attention pattern than generation. Existing sparse attention methods including MoBA optimize for generation throughput but ignore the structured, query-driven retrieval demands of editing tasks where the model must precisely locate and modify specific sections while maintaining global coherence.

Proposed Method: We extend MoBA's block-routing mechanism with an edit-aware router that conditions block selection on both the query tokens AND a diff-embedding representing the proposed local change. Specifically, we augment MoBA's gating network with a lightweight diff-encoder that embeds (original_span, proposed_change) pairs, biasing block selection toward contextually dependent sections. During training, we introduce an edit-consistency auxiliary loss that penalizes attending to blocks that don't contribute to coherent post-edit documents.

Experiments: (1) Long-document editing benchmarks (LongEdit, Contract-NLI revision tasks, arXiv paper revision); (2) Ablation comparing standard MoBA routing vs. diff-conditioned routing on edit coherence metrics; (3) Efficiency analysis at 32K/128K/512K token lengths; (4) Human evaluation of revision quality on legal and scientific documents; (5) Analysis of which blocks are selected pre/post diff-conditioning to validate the mechanism.

title: HieraMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention for Multi-Document Reasoning with Cross-Block Information Propagation
description:
Problem: MoBA selects relevant blocks independently per query token, but complex multi-document reasoning tasks (e.g., multi-hop QA, legal contract analysis) require synthesizing information across multiple non-contiguous evidence spans. Current block-level routing lacks mechanisms to propagate information between selected blocks, potentially missing cross-document inference chains.

Proposed Method: We introduce HieraMoBA, a two-level hierarchical attention mechanism. At the first level, we apply MoBA-style sparse block selection using learned routing. At the second level, we introduce a lightweight 'bridge attention' module that operates over the compressed representations (mean-pooled tokens) of all selected blocks, enabling explicit cross-block information exchange before final token-level attention. Bridge attention uses only O(k^2) computation where k is the number of selected blocks (typically 8-16), adding negligible overhead. During training, we introduce a multi-hop consistency loss that encourages routing to co-select blocks containing complementary evidence.

Experiments: (1) Multi-hop QA benchmarks: HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA with 32K-128K context via document padding; (2) Legal and scientific document analysis requiring cross-reference reasoning; (3) Ablations isolating bridge attention vs. routing loss contributions; (4) Routing visualization showing co-selection patterns across evidence spans; (5) Comparison against MoBA, full attention, and retrieval-augmented baselines on accuracy and FLOPs.

title: HierMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention with Adaptive Granularity for Multi-Scale Long-Context Reasoning
description:
Problem: MoBA partitions context into fixed-size blocks and routes queries to a static number of blocks, which may be suboptimal across diverse reasoning tasks requiring attention at multiple granularities simultaneously (e.g., a legal document analysis task needs both fine-grained clause-level and coarse-grained section-level attention). Fixed block sizes create an inductive bias that limits adaptability.

Proposed Method: HierMoBA introduces a hierarchical block structure where the context is simultaneously partitioned at multiple granularities (e.g., 512, 2048, 8192 tokens). Each attention head is assigned via a learned router to one granularity level plus a set of blocks at that level. A lightweight cross-scale aggregation module merges outputs from heads operating at different granularities. The router is trained end-to-end with a load-balancing auxiliary loss applied per granularity level. During inference, granularity selection can be pruned based on task type, enabling graceful efficiency-performance tradeoffs.

Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, LongBench, RULER at 32K-512K context lengths. (2) Ablation over number of granularity levels and block sizes. (3) Routing analysis to verify whether different tasks activate different granularity levels. (4) Throughput/latency comparison against MoBA, full attention, and window attention baselines on A100/H100 GPUs. (5) Continual pretraining from a 7B base model on long-context corpora.

title: MoBA-Graph: Mixture of Block Attention with Learned Topological Routing for Multi-Document Reasoning
description:
Problem: MoBA's block partitioning is positional (contiguous chunks), which is suboptimal for multi-document or retrieval-augmented tasks where relevant context is scattered non-contiguously across documents. The router has no awareness of document boundaries or cross-document relationships, potentially wasting capacity on intra-document noise while missing inter-document dependencies critical for complex reasoning.

Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Graph, which augments MoBA's block routing with a lightweight graph-structured prior. Documents are treated as nodes; an auxiliary shallow encoder computes pairwise relevance scores between document blocks, constructing a dynamic sparse attention graph. The MoE router is conditioned on both positional embeddings and graph-adjacency features, allowing it to route queries toward topologically related blocks rather than purely positionally proximate ones. During training, a graph-consistency auxiliary loss encourages routing decisions to align with retrieved document relevance signals. At inference, the graph can be constructed from metadata (citations, entity co-occurrence) or learned end-to-end.

Experiments: (1) Multi-hop QA benchmarks (HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA) in long-context retrieval settings; (2) RAG tasks with 100+ retrieved passages; (3) Ablations comparing positional-only vs. graph-conditioned routing; (4) Efficiency analysis (FLOPs, latency) vs. full attention and vanilla MoBA across 32K–256K token contexts; (5) Routing interpretability analysis showing cross-document attention patterns.

title: MoBA-Tree: Hierarchical Block Attention via Adaptive Tree-Structured Context Routing
description:
Problem: MoBA assigns query tokens to flat blocks of equal size, which ignores the natural hierarchical structure of long documents (sentences, paragraphs, sections). A flat block partition may split semantically coherent units or merge unrelated content, reducing the quality of sparse attention routing decisions—especially in multi-document reasoning, legal analysis, or scientific literature review.

Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Tree, which organizes the key-value context into a dynamic binary tree where leaf nodes are fine-grained token blocks and internal nodes store compressed representations (mean-pooled or learned summaries) of their subtrees. At inference, each query first routes through internal tree nodes using lightweight MoE gating, pruning entire subtrees before attending to selected leaf blocks. This yields O(log N) routing decisions and O(k) full attention blocks per query. During training, we add an auxiliary loss encouraging tree structure to align with sentence/paragraph boundaries detected by a lightweight segmenter. The gating network is trained end-to-end jointly with the LLM.

Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, LongBench, RULER at 32K–512K tokens. (2) Ablations: flat vs. tree routing, fixed vs. adaptive boundaries. (3) FLOPs vs. accuracy Pareto curves compared to MoBA, StreamingLLM, and SnapKV. (4) Case studies on multi-hop QA showing which tree levels are activated per query.

title: HierMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention with Adaptive Granularity for Multi-Scale Long-Context Reasoning
description: Problem: MoBA uses fixed-size blocks for sparse attention routing, but long documents naturally exhibit multi-scale structure (sentences, paragraphs, sections, documents). A uniform block size is suboptimal: fine-grained blocks waste computation on coarse semantic retrieval, while coarse blocks miss fine-grained dependencies critical for detailed reasoning tasks like multi-hop QA or code analysis. Proposed Method: We introduce HierMoBA, a hierarchical extension of MoBA that maintains a pyramid of block granularities simultaneously. Each attention head is assigned to a granularity level (fine/medium/coarse) via a learned routing mechanism. A lightweight hierarchical summarization module computes compressed representations at each level using a small transformer encoder. The MoE-style router selects top-k blocks across all granularity levels jointly, enabling queries to adaptively attend to both detailed nearby tokens and high-level distant context. A cross-level consistency loss encourages coherent routing across granularities. Planned Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, InfiniteBench, LongBench comparing against MoBA, full attention, and sink/window baselines; (2) Ablations on number of hierarchy levels and block size schedules; (3) Multi-hop reasoning tasks (HotpotQA-long, MuSiQue) to test fine-grained dependency capture; (4) Efficiency profiling (FLOPs, latency) at 32K-512K context lengths; (5) Analysis of routing patterns across hierarchy levels to validate multi-scale behavior.

title: HierMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention with Adaptive Granularity for Multi-Scale Long-Context Reasoning
description:
Problem: MoBA partitions context into fixed-size blocks, but optimal attention granularity varies across document structure (e.g., sentences vs. paragraphs vs. sections) and task type (e.g., needle-in-haystack vs. multi-hop reasoning). Fixed block sizes create a mismatch between attention routing and semantic boundaries, potentially routing queries to blocks that span irrelevant content.

Proposed Method: We introduce HierMoBA, which maintains multiple parallel block partitions at different granularities (fine: 128 tokens, medium: 512 tokens, coarse: 2048 tokens) and learns a meta-router that dynamically selects both the granularity level and the specific blocks to attend to for each query token. The meta-router is a lightweight 2-layer MLP trained end-to-end using a combined load-balancing and task-performance objective. At inference, each attention head independently selects granularity, enabling different heads to specialize at different scales. We also introduce semantic boundary snapping: blocks are softly adjusted to align with detected sentence/paragraph boundaries using a pretrained boundary detector.

Experiments: (1) RULER and LongBench benchmarks at 32K-256K context lengths; (2) ablation over fixed vs. adaptive granularity; (3) head specialization analysis showing emergent multi-scale behavior; (4) FLOPs/latency comparison against MoBA, NSA, and full attention baselines on A100 GPUs.

title: HieraMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention with Adaptive Granularity for Multi-Scale Long-Context Reasoning
description: Problem: MoBA partitions context into fixed-size blocks for sparse attention routing, but optimal block granularity varies across document types, reasoning tasks, and attention heads. Fixed blocks may miss fine-grained token-level dependencies in code reasoning or coarse document-level patterns in multi-hop QA simultaneously. Proposed Method: We introduce HieraMoBA, which extends MoBA by maintaining a two-level block hierarchy — coarse blocks (e.g., 2048 tokens) and fine blocks (e.g., 256 tokens). Each attention head receives a learned router that selects K_c coarse blocks and K_f fine blocks independently per query, enabling adaptive granularity. A lightweight head-specialization loss encourages diversity across heads, promoting some heads to specialize in coarse global routing and others in fine local retrieval. We further introduce a cross-level consistency regularizer ensuring that coarse block selections align with aggregated fine block selections. The architecture maintains MoBA's seamless full/sparse switching property. Experiments: We evaluate on LongBench, RULER (128K contexts), multi-hop QA (MuSiQue, HotpotQA), and code completion at 64K+ context lengths. We ablate granularity levels, router designs, and head specialization. Comparisons include MoBA, StreamingLLM, BigBird, and full attention baselines, measuring both accuracy and wall-clock efficiency on A100s.

title: MoBA-Graph: Adaptive Block Attention Routing for Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Document Reasoning
description:
Problem: Long-context LLMs processing multiple retrieved documents (e.g., 20-50 documents for complex QA or scientific synthesis) suffer from 'attention dilution'—the model cannot distinguish document boundaries or cross-document relationships, even with efficient sparse attention like MoBA. Standard block partitioning ignores semantic document structure, potentially splitting a block across document boundaries and wasting routing capacity on intra-document noise.

Proposed Method: We extend MoBA with document-aware block construction and a graph-guided routing mechanism. First, documents are treated as natural block units rather than fixed-size chunks, with variable block sizes aligned to document boundaries. Second, we introduce a lightweight cross-document dependency graph (built using BM25 and shallow embedding similarity at inference time) that biases the MoE routing gates—queries within a document attend preferentially to relevant retrieved documents rather than uniformly sampling sparse blocks. The gating remains learnable but receives the graph adjacency as a soft prior, preserving MoBA's 'less structure' spirit while exploiting retrieval metadata.

Experiments: (1) Multi-hop QA benchmarks (MuSiQue, HotpotQA-fullwiki, 2WikiMultiHopQA) with 32K–128K contexts; (2) Long-form scientific synthesis (SciRepEval); (3) Ablations on fixed vs. document-aligned blocks; (4) Routing entropy analysis to verify cross-document attention patterns; (5) Latency/throughput comparison against MoBA, full attention, and RAG-specific sparse transformers.

title: HierMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention with Adaptive Granularity for Multi-Scale Long-Context Reasoning
description:
Problem: MoBA assigns queries to fixed-size blocks uniformly, but real documents exhibit multi-scale structure (sentences, paragraphs, sections, chapters). A single block granularity forces a trade-off between fine-grained local precision and coarse global coverage, limiting performance on tasks requiring reasoning across multiple structural scales simultaneously (e.g., cross-chapter book QA, multi-hop scientific literature reasoning).

Proposed Method: HierMoBA introduces a hierarchical routing mechanism operating simultaneously at multiple block granularities (e.g., 512, 2048, 8192 tokens). Each query head routes to blocks at different levels of the hierarchy via a lightweight multi-scale router, aggregating outputs through learned level-wise gating. Critically, an adaptive granularity selector dynamically chooses which hierarchy levels to activate per query based on predicted information density, enabling compute savings. A compressed hierarchical KV-cache stores summarized representations for coarser levels, avoiding full recomputation.

Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, RULER, InfiniteBench, LongBench across 32K–1M token contexts. (2) Ablations on granularity combinations and routing overhead. (3) Comparison against MoBA, full attention, NSA, and StreamingLLM. (4) Efficiency profiling (FLOPs, wall-clock time) at varying context lengths. (5) Continued pretraining from a 7B base model with progressive context extension.

title: HierMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention for Multi-Granularity Long-Context Reasoning
description:
Problem: MoBA routes queries to fixed-size blocks at a single granularity, which may be suboptimal for tasks requiring reasoning across multiple temporal or semantic scales simultaneously (e.g., book-length QA requiring both local syntactic and global thematic attention). A single block size cannot efficiently capture both fine-grained token dependencies and coarse-grained document-level relationships.

Proposed Method: We introduce HierMoBA, a hierarchical extension where attention operates across two levels of block granularity simultaneously. At each layer, queries are routed via separate MoE-style gating to both fine-grained blocks (small, ~256 tokens) and coarse-grained blocks (large, ~2048 tokens represented by compressed summary tokens via mean/max pooling). A learned mixing coefficient combines outputs from both granularities, allowing the model to dynamically balance local and global context retrieval per query. Summary tokens are updated incrementally to avoid quadratic overhead. The architecture maintains MoBA's full-to-sparse transitional compatibility.

Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, RULER, LongBench across 32K-512K contexts. (2) Ablations on block granularity ratios and mixing coefficient behavior. (3) Computational profiling vs. MoBA, full attention, and sliding-window baselines. (4) Probing studies analyzing when fine vs. coarse routing dominates for different task types (retrieval vs. summarization vs. multi-hop reasoning). Models trained from 7B parameter checkpoints with progressive context length extension.

title: MoBA-Graph: Learned Block Routing for Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs
description: Problem: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over large knowledge graphs (KGs) requires attending to sparse, semantically relevant subgraphs scattered across massive contexts, yet existing long-context LLMs either waste compute attending uniformly or rely on hand-crafted retrieval heuristics that miss complex multi-hop reasoning chains. Method: We extend MoBA's block-routing principle to graph-structured contexts. Instead of partitioning a flat token sequence into blocks, we partition KG triples into semantically coherent blocks using entity clustering, then train a lightweight router—conditioned on query embeddings and block summary vectors—to dynamically select the top-k relevant triple blocks per attention head. The routing is end-to-end differentiable via straight-through estimation, and we augment the router with a graph-propagation step that biases block selection toward structurally adjacent blocks of already-selected ones, enabling multi-hop reasoning without exhaustive traversal. Experiments: (1) Multi-hop QA benchmarks (MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, WebQSP) with KG contexts serialized up to 64K tokens; (2) Comparison against full attention, window attention, MoBA (flat), and retrieval-augmented baselines; (3) Ablations on routing temperature, adjacency bias strength, and number of selected blocks; (4) Efficiency analysis (FLOPs, latency) at varying KG sizes. We expect MoBA-Graph to match full-attention accuracy while reducing compute by 4–6× on multi-hop reasoning tasks.

title: MoBA-Graph: Learned Block Attention Routing for Structured Document Understanding via Graph-Aware Context Partitioning
description:
Problem: Long-context LLMs processing structured documents (legal contracts, scientific papers, code repositories) suffer from inefficient attention because relevant information follows document-structure topology rather than positional proximity. MoBA's block partitioning treats all positions uniformly, missing opportunities to align sparse attention routing with semantic document structure.

Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Graph, which augments MoBA's block routing mechanism with a lightweight document-structure graph. During prefill, we parse structural signals (section headers, citation links, function call graphs, table references) into a sparse adjacency graph. The MoE router is then jointly trained to incorporate both content-based gating (as in MoBA) and graph-propagated structural affinity scores, allowing attention blocks to be selected based on structural relevance. We add a graph-conditioned positional bias term to the router's gating logits without modifying the core attention kernel, preserving hardware efficiency. A curriculum training strategy first trains on flat text (recovering standard MoBA), then fine-tunes on structured corpora.

Experiments: (1) Long-document QA benchmarks: QASPER, ContractNLI, LongCode-QA; (2) Ablation comparing flat-MoBA vs. MoBA-Graph routing quality; (3) Routing visualization showing structural vs. positional block selection patterns; (4) Efficiency analysis (FLOPs, latency) vs. full attention baselines at 32k–128k context lengths; (5) Zero-shot transfer across document domains.

title: MoBA-Graph: Adaptive Block Attention over Structured Knowledge for Multi-Hop Reasoning in Long-Context LLMs
description: Problem: While MoBA effectively reduces attention complexity via learned block routing, it treats all token positions uniformly without exploiting explicit structural relationships. Multi-hop reasoning tasks (e.g., complex QA over long documents, code dependency analysis) often have latent graph structures—entity co-references, logical dependencies, causal chains—that, if surfaced, could dramatically improve block selection quality and reasoning accuracy. Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Graph, which augments MoBA's gating mechanism with a lightweight, dynamically constructed token-level graph derived from sparse structural signals (entity linking, syntactic dependencies, code call graphs). Each query block's router receives additional graph-propagated embeddings (via 1-2 rounds of GNN message passing over the constructed graph) before selecting key-value blocks. This steers attention routing toward structurally relevant blocks rather than purely proximity-based ones. Critically, the graph construction is sparse and amortized, preserving MoBA's efficiency. The GNN component is jointly trained end-to-end. Experiments: (1) Multi-hop QA benchmarks (HotpotQA, MuSiQue) with contexts up to 128K tokens; (2) Long-context code reasoning (SWE-bench with full repository context); (3) Ablation of graph signal type and propagation depth; (4) Routing entropy analysis comparing MoBA vs MoBA-Graph block selection patterns; (5) Computational overhead profiling versus full attention and vanilla MoBA.

title: MoBA-Graph: Learned Sparse Attention over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs for Multi-Hop Reasoning
description:
Problem: Long-context LLMs struggle with multi-hop reasoning tasks (e.g., complex QA, scientific literature synthesis) where relevant information is scattered non-contiguously across thousands of tokens. MoBA's block-routing mechanism treats context as uniform chunks, but multi-hop reasoning requires attending to semantically linked but spatially distant evidence chains. Predefined block boundaries may arbitrarily split entity-relation structures critical for reasoning chains.

Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Graph, which augments MoBA's block-routing with a lightweight online graph construction module. During prefill, we extract entity-relation spans using a small auxiliary model to build a dynamic knowledge graph over the context. The MoBA router is extended to route queries not just to positional blocks but also to graph-neighborhood blocks—groups of tokens forming connected subgraphs around salient entities. A graph-aware block merging strategy dynamically re-chunks the context based on entity co-occurrence, ensuring reasoning-critical tokens cluster together. The gating mechanism incorporates both positional and semantic similarity signals.

Experiments: (1) Multi-hop QA benchmarks: MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHop with 32k–128k contexts; (2) Scientific synthesis tasks from LongBench-v2; (3) Ablations comparing positional-only vs. graph-augmented routing; (4) Efficiency analysis: FLOPs and latency vs. full attention and vanilla MoBA; (5) Routing interpretability: do graph-routed blocks align with gold evidence chains?

title: MoBA-Graph: Learned Sparse Attention via Dynamic Graph Topology for Multi-Document Reasoning
description:
Problem: MoBA partitions context into fixed contiguous blocks and routes queries to relevant blocks, but many long-context tasks (multi-hop QA, legal document analysis, scientific literature synthesis) exhibit non-contiguous, semantically structured dependencies where relevant information is scattered across distant, thematically linked passages rather than spatial blocks. Fixed block boundaries ignore document structure and cross-document relationships.

Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Graph, which replaces contiguous block partitioning with a dynamic document-graph topology. Documents/passages are treated as graph nodes; a lightweight GNN-based router learns to predict sparse attention edges between query tokens and relevant passage nodes based on semantic similarity and structural document metadata (citations, sections, entities). The router operates hierarchically: first selecting relevant documents, then relevant passages within them. Routing decisions are trained end-to-end with a differentiable top-k relaxation and an auxiliary load-balancing loss similar to MoE training.

Experiments: (1) Multi-hop reasoning benchmarks: MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA with 32K-128K context windows. (2) Legal multi-document QA (CUAD). (3) Scientific literature synthesis tasks. (4) Ablations: contiguous blocks vs. graph topology, fixed vs. learned routing, GNN depth. (5) Efficiency analysis: FLOPs and latency vs. MoBA, full attention, and sink attention at varying context lengths. Baseline comparisons include MoBA, LongFormer, and BigBird.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Expert Count Scheduling in Mixture of Block Attention for Variable-Length Long-Context Inference
description:
Problem: MoBA uses a fixed number of attended blocks (top-k selection) regardless of query complexity or sequence length, leading to suboptimal trade-offs — simple queries waste computation attending k blocks while complex multi-hop reasoning queries may need more. This rigidity limits efficiency gains without a principled way to allocate attention budget dynamically.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiMoBA, which augments MoBA with a lightweight complexity-aware gating controller that predicts per-query the optimal number of blocks to attend (k*) from {1,...,K_max}. The controller is a small MLP trained jointly with the LLM using a dual objective: task loss plus a sparsity regularization term penalizing unnecessary block selections. We additionally propose a token-level difficulty score derived from entropy of the router's block-selection logits, enabling dynamic k* at inference time without retraining via threshold tuning.

Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: RULER, LongBench, SCROLLS comparing fixed-k MoBA vs. AdaptiMoBA at equal average FLOPs budgets. (2) Multi-hop reasoning tasks (MuSiQue, HotpotQA-long) to test whether dynamic k helps complex queries. (3) Ablations on gating architecture, regularization strength, and k* distribution analysis. (4) Wall-clock inference speedup on 128K-token sequences across varying query complexity distributions. We expect 15-25% FLOP reduction at matched accuracy versus fixed-k MoBA.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Expert Count Scheduling in Mixture of Block Attention for Variable-Length Long-Context Inference
description:
Problem: MoBA uses a fixed number of attention blocks (experts) per query token throughout inference, ignoring that different layers, token positions, and task types require varying levels of contextual breadth. Early layers may need broad context while later layers benefit from focused attention; similarly, retrieval tasks differ from reasoning tasks in their attention patterns. This static allocation wastes computation in some contexts while under-attending in others.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiMoBA, which augments MoBA with a lightweight meta-controller that dynamically adjusts the number of selected block-experts (k) per layer and per token group during both training and inference. The meta-controller is a small MLP trained with a differentiable budget-aware loss that balances task performance against FLOPs consumption. We additionally propose layer-wise expert budgets informed by attention entropy statistics collected during a profiling phase, allowing high-entropy layers to receive more experts.

Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, HELMET, and Needle-in-Haystack with context lengths 32K–512K; (2) Ablation of dynamic vs. fixed k across layers; (3) FLOPs-accuracy Pareto curves comparing AdaptiMoBA against MoBA, StreamingLLM, and BigBird; (4) Analysis of learned k distributions across layers and task types to validate specialization; (5) Latency measurements on real hardware deployments.

title: MoBA-Graph: Adaptive Block Attention over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs for Multi-Hop Reasoning
description:
Problem: Long-context LLMs struggle with multi-hop reasoning over large knowledge graphs (KGs) embedded in context, where relevant facts are sparsely distributed and traditional attention wastes computation on irrelevant graph nodes. Existing graph-augmented LLMs either externalize graph traversal or use full attention over serialized KG tokens, both inefficient at scale.

Proposed Method: We extend MoBA's block-routing principle to KG-structured contexts by constructing attention blocks aligned with graph community structure (via hierarchical clustering of entity embeddings). A learned router directs each query token to attend only to K most relevant graph communities, plus a global sink block. Unlike vanilla MoBA's uniform spatial blocks, our blocks are semantically coherent graph neighborhoods, enabling the router to learn entity-relationship locality. We further introduce a graph-aware positional encoding that respects graph distance rather than sequential position, allowing the mechanism to distinguish structural proximity from textual proximity.

Experiments: (1) Multi-hop QA benchmarks: HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and 2WikiMultiHopQA with KG context serialized at 32K-128K tokens. (2) Ablations comparing uniform vs. graph-community blocks. (3) Routing analysis showing whether learned gates recover ground-truth reasoning paths. (4) Inference efficiency (FLOPs, latency) vs. full attention and sliding-window baselines at increasing graph sizes.

title: MoBA-Graph: Adaptive Block Attention with Learned Topology for Multi-Document Reasoning
description: Problem: MoBA's block partitioning assumes uniform token segmentation, which ignores semantic document boundaries in multi-document tasks (e.g., legal contract analysis, scientific literature synthesis). When relevant information spans structured units like paragraphs or documents, uniform blocks fragment semantic coherence, forcing attention routing to compensate for structurally arbitrary splits. Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Graph, which replaces MoBA's fixed uniform block partition with a learned hierarchical graph topology. At ingestion time, a lightweight boundary detector (fine-tuned sentence-BERT) segments input into semantic units (sentences, paragraphs, documents). A small GNN then learns inter-unit edge weights representing relevance priors. The MoE routing mechanism selects top-k semantic blocks rather than uniform positional blocks, with routing keys derived from block-level pooled representations. Crucially, the graph topology is differentiable and jointly trained end-to-end with the LLM via straight-through estimation, allowing the model to refine semantic boundaries during training. Experiments: (1) Multi-hop QA benchmarks (MuSiQue, HotpotQA-fullwiki) at 32k-128k context; (2) Legal NLI across multi-clause contracts; (3) Scientific claim verification over concatenated papers; (4) Ablations comparing uniform vs. semantic blocks and fixed vs. learned graph topology; (5) FLOPs/accuracy Pareto curves against MoBA and full attention baselines.

title: HieraMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention with Adaptive Granularity for Multi-Scale Long-Context Reasoning
description: Problem: MoBA partitions context into fixed-size blocks and routes queries to relevant blocks via a flat gating mechanism. However, long-context tasks exhibit multi-scale dependencies—some tokens need fine-grained local attention, others require coarse global context. Fixed block granularity creates a mismatch: too coarse misses local structure, too fine loses global coherence and increases routing overhead. Proposed Method: We introduce HieraMoBA, which maintains a hierarchy of block granularities (e.g., 256, 1024, 4096 tokens) simultaneously. A lightweight meta-router first decides the appropriate granularity level(s) for each query, then a per-level MoBA router selects top-k blocks at that scale. Blocks at coarser levels are represented by compressed key-value summaries (via learned pooling), enabling efficient cross-scale attention without materializing full KV caches at every level. A load-balancing auxiliary loss ensures routing diversity across scales. The architecture retains MoBA's seamless fallback to full attention during training. Planned Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks (SCROLLS, RULER, LongBench) comparing HieraMoBA against MoBA, StreamingLLM, and LongFormer at 32K–512K context lengths; (2) Ablations on granularity levels, compression ratios, and routing strategies; (3) Multi-hop reasoning tasks (HotpotQA, MuSiQue) to evaluate cross-scale dependency capture; (4) Wall-clock efficiency profiling on A100 GPUs across context lengths.

title: MoBA-Edit: Targeted Context Editing in Long Documents via Sparse Attention Routing Interpretability
description: Problem: When LLMs process long contexts using sparse attention mechanisms like MoBA, it remains unclear which blocks are consistently attended to for specific reasoning tasks, making targeted document editing (e.g., fact updates, debiasing) difficult without full re-inference. Understanding and exploiting MoBA's routing patterns could enable efficient, localized context modifications. Proposed Method: We analyze MoBA's block-routing decisions across diverse long-context tasks to build a 'routing fingerprint' — a lightweight map of which context blocks are critical for specific query types. We then propose MoBA-Edit, a method that (1) identifies minimally sufficient block subsets for a given query via routing statistics, (2) performs targeted gradient-based edits to only those blocks' key-value representations, and (3) verifies edit propagation without full re-computation. We introduce a trainable routing-conditioned editor module that predicts edit impact given routing patterns. Experiments: (1) Evaluate fact-editing accuracy on long-document QA (QuALITY, SCROLLS) comparing full-context editing vs. MoBA-guided sparse editing; (2) Measure edit efficiency (FLOPs, latency) vs. baseline re-inference; (3) Test edit locality — whether changes bleed into unrelated queries; (4) Ablate routing fingerprint granularity. This work bridges sparse attention efficiency with mechanistic interpretability for practical document maintenance.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Expert Count Scheduling in Mixture of Block Attention for Variable-Length Long-Context Inference
description: Problem: MoBA uses a fixed number of attended blocks (top-k selection) regardless of query complexity or sequence position, treating a simple factual lookup identically to multi-hop reasoning over a 128K context. This wastes compute for easy queries and under-allocates for complex ones. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiMoBA, which augments MoBA's block routing mechanism with a lightweight complexity estimator — a small MLP head trained jointly with the LM objective — that predicts per-query optimal block count k* at inference time. During training, we employ a differentiable annealing schedule over k with a sparsity regularization loss that penalizes unnecessary block activations while preserving task performance. A confidence-based early-exit criterion further gates whether full attention fallback is needed for specific attention heads. For efficient batched inference, we bin queries by predicted k* and process each bin with hardware-optimized kernels. Experiments: We evaluate on SCROLLS, LongBench, and RULER benchmarks across 7B and 13B parameter models fine-tuned from LLaMA-3. Ablations measure (1) FLOPs reduction vs. accuracy tradeoff curves, (2) correlation between estimated complexity and ground-truth difficulty labels, (3) latency profiling on A100/H100 GPUs at 32K–256K sequence lengths, and (4) comparison against fixed-k MoBA and NSA baselines.

title: MoBA-Tree: Hierarchical Block Attention Routing via Adaptive Tree Structures for Ultra-Long Context Reasoning
description: Problem: MoBA routes queries to flat, equal-sized blocks, which may be suboptimal for documents with hierarchical semantic structure (e.g., books with chapters/sections, codebases with files/functions). Equal block granularity forces a trade-off: large blocks waste capacity on irrelevant content while small blocks miss cross-chunk dependencies. Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Tree, which replaces flat block partitioning with a dynamically constructed multi-resolution tree over the context. Each leaf represents a fine-grained token window; internal nodes represent coarser summaries computed via lightweight pooling transformers. The MoE router operates over tree nodes rather than flat blocks, allowing a query to select either coarse summary nodes (broad semantic coverage, low cost) or fine leaf nodes (precise retrieval, higher cost) within a fixed compute budget. An auxiliary load-balancing loss encourages both granularities to be utilized. A progressive fallback mechanism allows seamless transition to full attention for critical tokens, inheriting MoBA's compatibility advantage. Experiments: (1) Long-context QA benchmarks (SCROLLS, InfiniteBench, RULER) against MoBA and other sparse attention baselines; (2) Multi-hop reasoning tasks requiring cross-section dependencies; (3) Ablations on tree depth, routing granularity mix, and compute-accuracy Pareto curves at 128K–1M token contexts; (4) Perplexity on hierarchically structured corpora (books, code).

title: HierMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention with Adaptive Granularity for Multi-Scale Long-Context Reasoning
description: Problem: MoBA partitions context into fixed-size blocks, which may misalign with the natural semantic granularity of documents (sentences, paragraphs, sections). When reasoning tasks require attending across multiple scales simultaneously—e.g., cross-referencing a sentence-level detail against a document-level thesis—uniform block sizes create routing inefficiencies and miss hierarchical structure. Proposed Method: We introduce HierMoBA, which maintains multiple block granularities (fine/medium/coarse) simultaneously and learns a two-level routing mechanism: first selecting granularity level, then selecting blocks at that level. Each attention head receives a budget of K total blocks drawn from a learned mixture across granularity levels, governed by a hierarchical MoE router with load-balancing constraints. The transition between full and sparse attention from MoBA is preserved, but now activates granularity-aware sparse patterns. A lightweight 'scale detector' module uses compressed representations to signal which granularity is most informative per query token. Planned Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, LongBench, Loong; (2) Multi-hop QA tasks requiring cross-scale evidence aggregation (HotpotQA extended to 128K context); (3) Ablations over granularity levels, routing overhead, and block budget allocation; (4) Efficiency profiling versus MoBA and full attention at 32K–512K context lengths; (5) Fine-tuning experiments initializing from MoBA-pretrained checkpoints.

title: MoBA-Graph: Adaptive Block Attention with Learned Topology for Multi-Document Reasoning
description:
Problem: MoBA routes queries to fixed-size contiguous blocks, which is suboptimal for multi-document tasks (e.g., multi-hop QA, legal contract analysis) where relevant context is scattered across semantically related but physically distant segments. Uniform block partitioning ignores document boundaries and cross-document relationships, forcing the router to discover structure that could be made explicit.

Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Graph, which augments MoBA's block routing with a lightweight graph-based topology layer. During prefill, documents are segmented into semantic units (paragraphs/sections). A small GNN or learned adjacency module constructs a sparse document graph based on entity overlap and embedding similarity. MoBA's gating mechanism is extended to treat graph neighborhoods as candidate blocks alongside contiguous blocks, selecting top-K blocks via combined positional and structural affinity scores. The graph topology is updated lazily (every N layers) to amortize cost. A straight-through estimator enables end-to-end training of the topology jointly with the LLM.

Experiments: (1) Multi-hop QA benchmarks: HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and 2WikiMultiHopQA with 32K–128K context via document padding. (2) Legal/scientific document understanding: QASPER, ContractNLI. (3) Ablations: graph vs. no-graph routing, GNN depth, update frequency. (4) Efficiency analysis: FLOPs and wall-clock vs. MoBA baseline and full attention. Hypothesis: graph-augmented routing achieves 5–10% accuracy gains on multi-hop tasks with <15% additional overhead over vanilla MoBA.

title: MoBA-Graph: Adaptive Block Attention Routing for Graph-Structured Long Documents
description:
Problem: Long-context LLMs struggle with documents having inherent graph structure (legal citations, scientific papers with references, codebases with dependencies), where relevant context follows graph topology rather than positional proximity. MoBA's block-based routing treats all blocks equally, missing opportunities to exploit known structural relationships between document segments.

Proposed Method: MoBA-Graph augments MoBA's routing mechanism with a lightweight graph-aware prior. Given a document with known or extractable inter-segment dependencies (citation graphs, import graphs, section cross-references), we construct a sparse adjacency signal injected into the MoE router as a soft bias term. The router learns to balance positional block relevance (original MoBA) with structural neighborhood relevance. A graph encoder (2-layer GNN) processes segment-level embeddings to produce routing logits that are additively combined with MoBA's content-based router scores. During inference, the graph structure can be pre-computed, adding minimal overhead.

Experiments: (1) Long legal document QA (multi-hop citation reasoning), (2) codebase question answering requiring cross-file dependency traversal, (3) scientific paper comprehension with cross-section references. Baselines: vanilla MoBA, full attention, window attention, GraphRAG. Ablations: graph prior strength, GNN depth, performance vs. context length scaling. Metric: accuracy, FLOP reduction vs. full attention.

title: HierMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention with Adaptive Granularity for Multi-Scale Long-Context Reasoning
description: Problem: MoBA partitions context into fixed-size blocks and routes queries to relevant blocks via MoE-style gating. However, real-world long-context tasks (e.g., multi-hop legal reasoning, scientific literature synthesis) require attending to information at multiple granularities simultaneously — fine-grained token-level details and coarse document-level summaries — which uniform block partitioning cannot capture efficiently. Method: We propose HierMoBA, which constructs a two-level block hierarchy: (1) fine-grained blocks of fixed size (e.g., 512 tokens) and (2) coarse-grained super-blocks formed by pooling representations from K consecutive fine blocks via learned compression tokens. Each query layer independently routes through both levels using separate MoE gates, allocating a budget of fine-block slots and super-block slots. A lightweight cross-level consistency loss encourages the coarse routing to subsume fine routing decisions, enabling graceful degradation. The architecture retains MoBA's compatibility with full-attention fallback. Experiments: We evaluate on SCROLLS, InfiniteBench, and HELMET benchmarks at context lengths 32K–512K, comparing against MoBA, StreamingLLM, and BigBird baselines. We also measure routing entropy across levels to analyze emergent multi-scale attention patterns and conduct ablations on budget allocation between fine/coarse levels and compression token count.

title: MoBA-KV: Dynamic Block-Sparse KV Cache Eviction via Mixture-of-Experts Routing for Memory-Efficient Long-Context Inference
description:
Problem: While MoBA reduces attention computation during training via sparse block routing, inference-time memory remains bottlenecked by storing full KV caches for all tokens. For 1M+ context windows, KV cache memory dominates GPU allocation, limiting deployment. Existing KV eviction methods (H2O, SnapKV) rely on fixed heuristics inconsistent with the learned routing structure of MoBA.

Proposed Method: We propose MoBA-KV, which repurposes MoBA's block-level attention router as a principled KV cache eviction signal. During inference, each query's router scores across blocks serve as importance weights for retaining or evicting KV cache blocks. We introduce a hierarchical retention policy: (1) a hard budget per attention head retaining top-K highest-routed blocks, (2) a global cross-layer consolidation where blocks consistently unselected across layers are freed from memory, and (3) a lightweight predictor that prefetches likely-to-be-reactivated blocks based on query embedding similarity. This creates a dynamic, structure-aware cache that evolves with the input stream.

Experiments: We evaluate on RULER, LongBench, and Needle-in-a-Haystack benchmarks at 128K–1M token contexts, measuring perplexity, task accuracy, peak GPU memory, and throughput. Baselines include H2O, SnapKV, StreamingLLM, and full MoBA. Ablations examine eviction granularity, prefetch accuracy, and cross-layer consolidation frequency.

title: MoBA-Tree: Hierarchical Block Attention Routing via Adaptive Token Clustering for Ultra-Long Context Reasoning
description:
Problem: MoBA assigns queries to fixed-size, position-contiguous blocks, which may not capture semantic coherence in long documents where relevant information is scattered non-contiguously. For tasks like multi-hop reasoning over 1M+ token contexts, a flat block partitioning scheme may force the router to select many blocks to cover semantically related but positionally distant content, undermining sparsity benefits.

Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Tree, which replaces static positional blocks with dynamically constructed hierarchical token clusters built via lightweight online agglomerative clustering of key embeddings. At inference time, tokens are organized into a two-level tree: fine-grained semantic clusters at leaves and coarse topic groups at internal nodes. The MoE-style router first selects top-k coarse clusters, then top-m fine clusters within them, enabling logarithmic-depth retrieval of semantically relevant tokens. A differentiable soft routing loss encourages cluster coherence during training. The transition to full attention is preserved for short contexts.

Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, HELMET, InfiniteBench, BABILong at 128K–1M tokens; (2) Ablations on cluster granularity, routing depth, and block count vs. MoBA baseline; (3) FLOPs/latency analysis on A100s; (4) Multi-hop QA stress tests measuring whether semantic clustering reduces required active blocks versus positional blocking.

title: MoBA-Graph: Adaptive Block Attention with Learned Topology for Multi-Document Reasoning
description: Problem: Long-context tasks involving multiple interleaved documents (e.g., multi-hop QA, legal reasoning over case collections) have inherent cross-document dependency structure that flat block partitioning in MoBA ignores. Blocks defined by position may fragment logically coherent units (paragraphs, sections) and miss cross-document connections that are critical for reasoning. Proposed Method: MoBA-Graph extends MoBA by replacing fixed positional block partitioning with a learned graph-structured block assignment. During preprocessing, a lightweight learned segmentation module clusters token spans into semantically coherent blocks using contrastive document-level embeddings. A second component learns a sparse inter-block routing graph (analogous to MoE gating) where each query block attends to its K nearest neighbor blocks in semantic space plus a global sink, rather than relying solely on positional proximity. The routing graph is end-to-end differentiable via straight-through Gumbel-softmax. This preserves MoBA's seamless full/sparse attention transitioning while injecting document-structure awareness. Planned Experiments: (1) Multi-hop QA benchmarks: HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA with 32k-128k context windows; (2) Legal multi-document summarization; (3) Ablations comparing positional blocks vs. semantic blocks vs. graph-routed blocks; (4) FLOPs vs. accuracy tradeoff curves against MoBA, full attention, and Longformer baselines; (5) Visualization of learned routing graphs to interpret cross-document attention patterns.

title: MoBA-Graph: Adaptive Block Attention over Structured Knowledge Graphs for Multi-Hop Reasoning
description: Problem: Long-context LLMs struggle with multi-hop reasoning over large knowledge graphs (KGs) serialized into text, where relevant facts are sparsely distributed and semantically clustered. Standard attention wastes compute on irrelevant triples, while existing sparse attention methods lack structural awareness of graph topology. Method: We propose MoBA-Graph, which extends MoBA's block-routing mechanism to incorporate KG structural priors. Instead of uniform partitioning into blocks, we partition serialized KG contexts using graph community detection (Louvain algorithm), creating semantically coherent blocks aligned with entity neighborhoods. A lightweight router network augmented with entity-relation embeddings learns to select relevant graph communities per query token, enabling structure-aware sparse attention. During training, we introduce a graph-topology auxiliary loss that encourages the router to select blocks containing entities within k hops of query entities, providing inductive bias without hard constraints. We further propose a progressive densification strategy: starting from sparse community attention and selectively enabling full attention for high-confidence reasoning chains. Experiments: We evaluate on multi-hop QA benchmarks (MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA) with KGs serialized at 32K-128K tokens, plus KGQA benchmarks (WebQSP, ComplexWebQuestions). We compare against MoBA, StreamingLLM, and full attention, measuring accuracy, FLOPs, and routing interpretability via entity-hop alignment scores.

title: MoBA-Graph: Learned Sparse Attention Topology Discovery via Graph Neural Networks for Structured Long-Document Reasoning
description:
Problem: MoBA routes queries to blocks uniformly via hashing or learned gating, but ignores the inherent hierarchical and relational structure present in long documents (e.g., legal contracts, scientific papers, codebases).
