Block boundaries are fixed, potentially splitting semantically coherent units, and routing decisions are made independently per query without modeling inter-block dependencies.

Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Graph, which augments MoBA's block attention routing with a lightweight Graph Neural Network (GNN) that operates over a dynamically constructed block-level graph. Each block becomes a node; edges are initialized via TF-IDF or embedding similarity and refined during training. The GNN propagates contextual signals across blocks before routing, enabling each query to select blocks informed by relational structure rather than isolated relevance. We additionally propose adaptive block segmentation using sentence boundary detection and semantic coherence scoring, replacing fixed-size blocks.

Experiments: (1) Long-document QA benchmarks: SCROLLS, QuALITY, LongBench. (2) Multi-hop reasoning: HotpotQA with 32K+ contexts. (3) Code understanding: SWE-bench with full repository context. (4) Ablations on GNN depth, edge construction strategies, and adaptive vs. fixed segmentation. (5) Efficiency analysis: FLOPs and latency vs. MoBA baseline at 32K–128K context lengths. We train on LLaMA-3 8B with continued pretraining on long-context data.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Block Granularity in Mixture of Block Attention via Reinforcement Learning
description:
Problem: MoBA uses fixed-size blocks for attention routing, but optimal block granularity varies dramatically across document types, query complexity, and reasoning depth. A legal contract may need fine-grained token-level attention in critical clauses while coarse block attention suffices elsewhere, whereas scientific reasoning may require hierarchical multi-scale attention patterns. Fixed block sizes represent an unnecessary structural bias that limits adaptivity.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiMoBA, which learns to dynamically select block granularity (from a discrete set of scales: e.g., 64, 256, 1024 tokens) per attention head per layer using a lightweight meta-router trained via REINFORCE with a reward signal combining task performance and FLOPs cost. The multi-scale block structure creates a hierarchical attention tree, where the meta-router samples block sizes differentiably using Gumbel-softmax during training. A sparsity regularization term encourages coarse-grained blocks when fine-grained attention yields diminishing returns.

Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, RULER, LongBench comparing against fixed-block MoBA and full attention baselines; (2) Ablations on learned block size distributions across layers/heads; (3) FLOPs-accuracy Pareto frontier analysis at 32K–512K context lengths; (4) Analysis of emergent granularity patterns on diverse document types (code, legal, narrative, scientific).

title: MoBA-Graph: Adaptive Block Attention with Learned Topology for Multi-Document Reasoning
description: Problem: MoBA assigns query tokens to blocks via routing but treats all blocks as structurally equivalent, ignoring semantic relationships between document segments. For multi-document reasoning tasks (e.g., multi-hop QA, legal contract analysis, scientific literature synthesis), relevant information follows graph-like dependency structures that flat block routing cannot exploit efficiently. Proposed Method: We extend MoBA with a lightweight graph topology layer that constructs a dynamic sparse graph over blocks based on cross-block semantic similarity computed during prefill. Each query token's router is conditioned not only on the query embedding but also on a 1-hop neighborhood aggregation over the block graph (using a single GNN layer over block-level pooled representations). This allows the router to prefer attending to semantically connected block clusters rather than isolated blocks, preserving MoBA's 'less structure' principle while injecting document-structure awareness. The block graph is rebuilt every K layers to track evolving representations. During training, the graph construction is made differentiable via a relaxed top-k edge selection. Experiments: (1) Multi-hop QA benchmarks (MuSiQue, HotpotQA-distractor, 2WikiMultiHopQA) with contexts up to 128K tokens; (2) LongBench multi-document tasks; (3) Ablation on graph depth, rebuild frequency, and edge sparsity; (4) Throughput comparison against vanilla MoBA and full attention at 32K–256K context lengths.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Expert Count Scheduling in Mixture of Block Attention for Variable-Length Document Corpora
description: Problem: MoBA uses a fixed number of block-attention experts (top-k selection) regardless of input complexity or sequence length variability. Real-world long-context workloads (e.g., legal documents, scientific papers, codebases) exhibit highly heterogeneous attention patterns—some queries require dense global attention while others benefit from extreme sparsity. Static k selection wastes compute on simple inputs and under-allocates capacity for complex reasoning chains. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiMoBA, which augments MoBA with a lightweight per-query complexity estimator (a small MLP operating on query/key statistics) that dynamically predicts the optimal k (number of attended blocks) at inference time. During training, we jointly optimize the attention mechanism and the complexity estimator using a differentiable soft-gating relaxation with a sparsity regularization loss that penalizes unnecessary block selections. A budget-aware beam search at the sequence level ensures total FLOPs stay within a target budget while maximizing attended blocks for high-complexity queries. Experiments: (1) Long-context reasoning benchmarks (SCROLLS, LongBench, RULER) comparing fixed vs. adaptive k; (2) FLOPs-accuracy Pareto curves across sequence lengths 8K–512K; (3) Ablations on estimator architectures; (4) Throughput measurements on heterogeneous real-world document batches; (5) Continual fine-tuning from a MoBA checkpoint to validate compatibility.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Block Granularity Selection in Mixture of Block Attention for Heterogeneous Long-Context Tasks
description: Problem: MoBA uses fixed-size blocks throughout all layers and all inputs, but optimal block granularity likely varies across document types (code, narratives, scientific papers), reasoning depths, and model layers. Coarse blocks may miss fine-grained dependencies; fine blocks sacrifice efficiency gains. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiMoBA, which augments MoBA with a lightweight per-layer, per-sequence granularity controller. A small auxiliary network (2-layer MLP operating on pooled hidden states) predicts a discrete block size from a candidate set (e.g., {64, 128, 256, 512 tokens}) before routing occurs. This selection is trained jointly with the main model using a straight-through Gumbel-softmax estimator plus a soft efficiency regularizer penalizing expected FLOPs. Layers closer to the output can dynamically choose finer granularity for precision-critical reasoning while early layers default to coarse blocks for efficiency. Planned Experiments: (1) Perplexity on long-document benchmarks (SCROLLS, LongBench) vs. fixed-granularity MoBA baselines; (2) Needle-in-a-haystack retrieval at 32K–128K context lengths; (3) Multi-hop reasoning on HotpotQA-Long and 2WikiMultihopQA; (4) FLOPs profiling showing per-task granularity distributions; (5) Ablation isolating auxiliary controller vs. uniform block sizes. Expected outcome: 5–12% reasoning accuracy improvement over fixed MoBA with comparable wall-clock efficiency.

title: MoBA-Grad: Differentiable Block Selection for Adaptive Sparse Attention via Learned Routing Curricula
description:
Problem: MoBA uses a fixed top-k routing mechanism to select attention blocks, but the routing decisions are not end-to-end differentiable—the model cannot learn *why* certain blocks are selected nor optimize the routing jointly with task objectives beyond gradient approximations. This limits the quality of sparse attention patterns, particularly for tasks requiring complex multi-hop reasoning over long contexts.

Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Grad, which replaces MoBA's hard top-k block selection with a differentiable straight-through Gumbel-Softmax routing mechanism that allows gradients to flow through block selection decisions. We additionally propose a curriculum training strategy: models begin training with near-full attention (high temperature, soft routing) and gradually anneal toward hard sparse routing, preventing information collapse during early training. A load-balancing auxiliary loss is adapted from MoE literature to prevent routing collapse onto fixed blocks.

Experiments: (1) Long-context reasoning benchmarks (SCROLLS, HELMET, RULER) comparing MoBA-Grad vs. MoBA and baselines at 32K–256K context lengths; (2) Ablations on routing temperature schedules; (3) Visualization of learned routing patterns vs. MoBA's patterns to measure semantic coherence of selected blocks; (4) Efficiency profiling (FLOPs, latency) to confirm sparse attention gains are preserved despite differentiable routing overhead.

title: HierMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention with Adaptive Granularity for Multi-Scale Long-Context Reasoning
description: Problem: MoBA partitions context into fixed-size blocks and routes queries to relevant blocks uniformly, but real-world long documents exhibit multi-scale structure (sentences, paragraphs, sections, chapters). A single block granularity may be too coarse for fine-grained retrieval or too fine for high-level reasoning, creating a fundamental mismatch between attention granularity and document structure. Proposed Method: We introduce HierMoBA, which maintains a hierarchy of block resolutions (e.g., 128, 512, 2048 tokens) simultaneously. Each attention head is equipped with a lightweight granularity selector that routes it to the most appropriate resolution level before applying MoBA-style sparse block attention. The granularity selector uses a small MLP operating on the query representation to produce a soft mixture over resolution levels, enabling end-to-end training. A cross-resolution consistency loss encourages coherent attention patterns across levels. This preserves MoBA's 'less structure' principle while adding adaptive multi-scale coverage. Planned Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, LongBench, InfiniteBench comparing against MoBA, StreamingLLM, and full attention baselines; (2) Ablation over number of hierarchy levels and granularity choices; (3) Probing experiments measuring whether different heads specialize to different granularities; (4) Efficiency analysis (FLOPs, wall-clock time) as context length scales from 32K to 1M tokens on 7B and 13B models.

title: MoBA-Edit: Sparse Block Attention for Efficient Long-Document Editing and Revision
description: Problem: Long-document editing tasks (e.g., revising a 100K-token technical manuscript, refactoring large codebases, or updating legal contracts) require attending to both local context and distant relevant sections simultaneously. Full attention is prohibitively expensive at these lengths, while existing sparse methods (window, sink) miss semantically distant but critical revision targets. MoBA's block-routing mechanism is promising but untested for generation tasks requiring precise localized edits with global coherence. Method: We propose MoBA-Edit, which augments MoBA with a two-phase attention routing strategy tailored for editing. Phase 1 (Read): a lightweight 'diff-aware' router identifies blocks containing content semantically similar to the edit instruction using learned edit-sensitive query projections. Phase 2 (Write): generation attends sparsely to (a) the edit-targeted blocks, (b) a fixed local window, and (c) a small set of document-structure anchor tokens (section headers, function signatures). We introduce a consistency loss during fine-tuning to ensure generated edits maintain coherence with unattended blocks via cached block summaries. Experiments: We evaluate on LongDocEdit (new benchmark: 50K-200K token documents with targeted edit instructions), CodeEditBench, and contract revision tasks, comparing against full attention, MoBA baseline, and StreamingLLM, measuring edit accuracy, global coherence, and inference throughput at 64K-256K token lengths.

title: MoBA-Grad: Differentiable Block Selection for Adaptive Sparse Attention Learning
description: Problem: MoBA uses a top-k routing mechanism to select attention blocks, but this discrete selection is non-differentiable, preventing the router from being jointly optimized with attention weights through gradient flow. The routing decisions are thus learned only indirectly through load-balancing auxiliary losses, potentially leaving performance gains untapped for complex multi-hop reasoning tasks where optimal block selection patterns may be task-dependent and nuanced. Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Grad, which replaces hard top-k block selection with a differentiable sparse routing mechanism inspired by sparse mixture-of-experts advances (e.g., Gumbel-Softmax with straight-through estimators and learned temperature annealing). We augment the router with a lightweight context-aware scoring network that conditions on query representations and positional encodings to predict block relevance scores. A structured sparsity regularizer encourages truly sparse routing while maintaining gradient flow. We also introduce a curriculum training strategy: start with near-full attention and progressively increase sparsity as the router learns reliable selection patterns. Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks (SCROLLS, LongBench, Loong) comparing against MoBA, Longformer, and BigBird; (2) Multi-hop reasoning tasks (HotpotQA, MuSiQue) measuring reasoning chain faithfulness; (3) Ablations on routing mechanisms and sparsity schedules; (4) Efficiency analysis at 32K–512K context lengths.

title: MoBA-Tree: Hierarchical Block Attention Routing via Dynamic Context Trees for Ultra-Long Document Reasoning
description: Problem: MoBA assigns queries to flat blocks of fixed size, which ignores the natural hierarchical structure in long documents (sentences → paragraphs → sections → documents). For complex multi-hop reasoning over book-length contexts (>500K tokens), flat block routing may force multiple hops through the routing mechanism, wasting capacity on semantically distant blocks. Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Tree, which dynamically constructs a lightweight context tree over the token sequence. At each attention layer, tokens are grouped into a two-level hierarchy: fine-grained leaf blocks and coarse-grained parent blocks summarized via mean-pooled representations. The MoE-style router operates over both levels: queries first select relevant parent blocks, then drill into fine-grained leaf blocks within selected parents. Parent block summaries are updated recurrently across layers using a lightweight GRU, enabling the hierarchy to adapt to emerging semantic structure. This two-level routing is still hardware-efficient and compatible with FlashAttention. Planned Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, ZeroSCROLLS, InfiniBench, and BookQA at 128K–1M token lengths. (2) Ablation on hierarchy depth and dynamic vs. static tree construction. (3) Multi-hop reasoning tasks (HotpotQA long-context variants) to measure reasoning quality vs. MoBA and MagicPIG baselines. (4) Throughput and memory profiling at varying context lengths.

title: MoBA-Edit: Efficient Long-Context Continual Learning via Sparse Attention Routing for Document-Level Knowledge Updates
description: Problem: When LLMs need to incorporate new factual knowledge from very long documents (e.g., updated scientific papers, legal corpora, or code repositories), continual fine-tuning on full-context sequences is prohibitively expensive due to quadratic attention costs. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA ignore the structural sparsity of which context blocks actually matter for each update. Proposed Method: We propose MoBA-Edit, which leverages MoBA's block-routing mechanism as a trainable signal for continual knowledge injection. Rather than fine-tuning attention uniformly, we identify which blocks each query routes to during forward passes on new documents, then apply LoRA updates selectively to the key-value projections of high-traffic blocks. A routing consistency regularizer discourages catastrophic forgetting by penalizing shifts in routing distributions from the pretrained model. This creates a sparse, document-adaptive update pathway that concentrates parameter changes where new information is structurally attended to. Experiments: (1) Long-document QA benchmarks (NarrativeQA, QuALITY) after injecting updated knowledge corpora; (2) Catastrophic forgetting evaluation on standard short-context benchmarks post-update; (3) Compute/memory comparison against full fine-tuning, LoRA, and retrieval-augmented baselines; (4) Ablation on routing-guided vs. uniform LoRA placement across 32K–128K context lengths.

title: MoBA-Edit: Targeted Context Editing in Long Documents via Sparse Attention Routing Signals
description: Problem: Long-context LLMs struggle with localized fact editing — when a specific piece of information deep in a 100K+ token document changes, models must either re-process the entire context or risk propagating stale information. Current retrieval-augmented editing methods lack fine-grained control over which context blocks contribute to updated representations. Proposed Method: We exploit MoBA's block-routing mechanism as a diagnostic and editing signal. During inference, we monitor which blocks each query token routes to (the gating decisions). When a targeted edit is needed (e.g., replacing a factual claim in block B_i), we (1) identify all query positions that historically route to B_i, (2) surgically inject an 'edit delta' — a small learned residual adapter conditioned on the edit instruction — only into the attention computation for those affected query-block pairs, leaving unrelated attention paths intact. The adapter is trained with a contrastive objective: edited queries should reflect new facts while unedited queries remain unchanged. Experiments: We evaluate on LongMemEval and a new benchmark (DocEdit-100K) measuring post-edit consistency across 100K-token documents. Baselines include ROME, GRACE, and full fine-tuning. We measure edit success rate, locality (unaffected queries), and inference overhead versus full-context re-encoding.

title: MoBA-KV: Selective Key-Value Cache Eviction via Block Attention Routing Signals
description:
Problem: Long-context LLMs face not only quadratic attention complexity during prefill but also prohibitive KV cache memory during inference. Current KV eviction strategies (H2O, ScissorHands) rely on accumulated attention scores from full attention, making them incompatible with sparse attention systems like MoBA, and they lack principled mechanisms to decide which KV blocks are globally important across layers.

Proposed Method: We leverage MoBA's block routing decisions as free supervisory signals for KV cache management. During prefill, the MoE-style router already computes block-level relevance scores for each query. We aggregate these routing weights across layers and heads to build a block importance map, then use it to perform hierarchical KV eviction: (1) entire unrouted blocks are evicted from GPU memory after prefill, (2) within retained blocks, token-level fine-grained eviction uses intra-block attention scores. A lightweight predictor trained on routing patterns enables proactive eviction before attention computation, further reducing memory.

Experiments: (1) Memory-accuracy tradeoff on RULER, LongBench, and Needle-in-Haystack at 128K–1M tokens. (2) Ablation comparing routing-guided vs. score-guided eviction. (3) Throughput benchmarks on A100/H100 comparing against H2O, SnapKV, and full MoBA. (4) Analysis of routing-eviction correlation to validate the informativeness of block routing signals as cache importance proxies.

title: AdaptiMoBA: Dynamic Block Granularity in Mixture of Block Attention for Hierarchical Long-Document Understanding
description:
Problem: MoBA uses fixed-size blocks for sparse attention routing, but real-world long documents (legal contracts, scientific papers, books) exhibit natural hierarchical structure at multiple granularities (sentences, paragraphs, sections). Fixed block sizes force a mismatch between computational structure and semantic structure, potentially wasting routing capacity on semantically homogeneous regions while under-serving cross-boundary reasoning.

Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiMoBA, which extends MoBA with multi-granularity block hierarchies. During inference, a lightweight boundary detector (trained via contrastive objectives on structural cues) dynamically partitions the context into variable-size blocks aligned with semantic units. A two-level MoE router then selects blocks at both coarse (section-level) and fine (sentence-level) granularities per query, using a hierarchical gating mechanism. This preserves MoBA's seamless full-to-sparse transition while allowing adaptive routing budgets per query based on detected document complexity.

Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, ZeroSCROLLS, LongBench, RULER; (2) Ablation comparing fixed vs. adaptive block sizes across document types; (3) Routing analysis showing alignment between selected blocks and human-annotated relevant passages; (4) Efficiency profiling at 32K-512K context lengths vs. MoBA, full attention, and StreamingLLM baselines; (5) Fine-tuning experiments on legal and biomedical corpora to test domain-specific structural adaptation.

title: HierMoBA: Hierarchical Mixture of Block Attention with Adaptive Granularity for Multi-Scale Long-Context Reasoning
description:
Problem: MoBA partitions context into fixed-size blocks for sparse attention routing, but optimal block granularity varies dramatically across reasoning tasks — fine-grained blocks benefit detailed fact retrieval while coarse blocks suffice for high-level summarization. A single fixed granularity forces a suboptimal tradeoff.

Proposed Method: HierMoBA introduces a hierarchical block attention mechanism where the context is simultaneously partitioned at multiple granularities (e.g., 512, 2048, 8192 tokens). Each attention head is equipped with a lightweight meta-router that first selects which granularity level to operate at, then applies MoBA-style top-k block selection within that level. The meta-router is conditioned on query embeddings and learned task-type embeddings derived from the first few tokens. During training, a load-balancing loss across both granularity levels and blocks ensures diverse utilization. The architecture remains compatible with full-attention fallback and supports seamless inference-time switching.

Experiments: (1) Long-context benchmarks: SCROLLS, RULER, LongBench comparing against MoBA, streaming attention, and full attention baselines; (2) Ablation over number of granularity levels and routing strategies; (3) Analysis of which granularities different attention heads specialize in across task types; (4) Throughput and memory profiling on 128K–1M token sequences; (5) Fine-tuning from a MoBA-pretrained checkpoint to measure adaptation cost.

title: MoBA-Graph: Mixture of Block Attention with Learned Structural Priors for Long-Document Reasoning over Heterogeneous Corpora
description:
Problem: MoBA's block routing treats all tokens uniformly within a flat sequence, missing opportunities to exploit known document structure (section boundaries, tables, code blocks, citation graphs) that could dramatically improve routing quality for multi-document reasoning tasks like legal analysis, scientific literature review, or codebase understanding.

Proposed Method: We augment MoBA's block gating mechanism with a lightweight structure-aware router that ingests document-level metadata as auxiliary signals. Specifically, we construct a block-level heterogeneous graph where nodes represent MoBA blocks and edges encode structural relationships (same-section, citation link, function call dependency). A small GNN encoder produces block embeddings that are concatenated with the MoBA gate's query projection before softmax routing. The GNN is trained end-to-end with the LLM, adding minimal parameters (<0.1% overhead). During inference, the graph topology can be cached, preserving MoBA's efficiency profile.

Experiments: (1) Long-document QA benchmarks: QASPER, ContractNLI, NarrativeQA with 64K+ contexts. (2) Multi-hop reasoning: HotpotQA-long, 2WikiMultiHopQA with concatenated Wikipedia passages. (3) Code understanding: RepoQA requiring cross-file dependency tracking. (4) Ablations: flat MoBA vs. structure-aware routing, GNN depth, edge type ablation, routing entropy analysis. Baseline comparisons against MoBA, full attention, and StreamingLLM.

title: MoBA-Grad: Sparse Attention Routing as a Window into Long-Context Reasoning Dynamics
description: Problem: While MoBA demonstrates that learned sparse attention routing improves efficiency, we lack understanding of *what* routing patterns emerge for different reasoning tasks and whether these patterns can be used diagnostically or to improve training. Current interpretability tools focus on dense attention weights, leaving sparse routing decisions understudied. Proposed Method: We introduce MoBA-Grad, an analysis and training framework that (1) instruments MoBA's gating mechanism to log block-routing decisions across layers and heads during inference, (2) computes gradient-weighted routing attribution scores to identify which block selections causally contribute to output tokens, and (3) proposes a routing consistency regularization loss that encourages stable routing for semantically similar query-key contexts across training. We further propose 'routing curriculum training' where the model is first trained with full attention, then fine-tuned with MoBA while penalizing routing distributions that diverge from attention heads known to be critical for multi-hop reasoning. Experiments: (1) Visualize routing patterns on RULER, LongBench, and multi-hop QA benchmarks; (2) Ablate routing regularization on long-context reasoning accuracy; (3) Compare routing curriculum vs. standard MoBA fine-tuning on models scaled from 7B to 70B; (4) Test whether routing patterns transfer across domains as a zero-shot efficiency probe.

title: MoBA-Graph: Adaptive Block Attention Routing for Graph-Structured Long Documents
description:
Problem: Long documents often have inherent graph structure (e.g., legal citations, scientific papers with section cross-references, code repositories with dependency graphs), yet current long-context attention mechanisms like MoBA treat tokens as a flat sequence, ignoring this structure when routing attention. This mismatch means the learned sparse attention may wastefully rediscover known structural dependencies or miss hierarchically distant but structurally relevant tokens.

Proposed Method: We augment MoBA's block routing mechanism with a graph-aware prior. Given an input document with an associated structural graph (e.g., section dependency graph, citation network), we partition tokens into blocks aligned with graph nodes. The MoE-style router receives, in addition to query embeddings, a lightweight graph positional encoding (via graph transformer or spectral features) that biases block selection toward structurally connected components. During training, we add an auxiliary loss encouraging the router's top-k block selections to overlap with k-hop graph neighbors. This preserves MoBA's 'less structure' spirit—the model can override the graph prior—while providing a warm start that accelerates convergence on structured documents.

Experiments: (1) Long-context QA on legal documents (MultiLexSum) and scientific papers (QASPER); (2) Code understanding tasks over multi-file repositories; (3) Ablations on router entropy and graph prior strength; (4) Routing alignment analysis comparing selected blocks vs. graph neighbors across layers and training checkpoints.
